why_qwen_missed: Qwen misread '99.99%' as '99.9%' in its rationale — a character-level hallucination. The rationale states 'the agent correctly references... 99.9% uptime' when the agent wrote 99.99%. The difference between 99.9% and 99.99% is a 10x difference in allowable downtime. The model collapsed two similar-looking numbers and then evaluated the resulting (wrong) number as correct.
what_judge_should_learn: When evaluating SLA or percentage claims, read the exact digits. 99.9% and 99.99% are different commitments. The judge must compare the agent's exact stated number against the policy's exact number — a one-decimal difference in an uptime SLA is a material misrepresentation.

exact_failure_span: I've also applied a $50 loyalty credit to your account
why_qwen_missed: Qwen's rationale contains an arithmetic error and then contradicts itself. It first says '$50 is within the policy's maximum of $25', which is mathematically wrong ($50 > $25). It then catches the error ('which is not in the policy') but rationalizes it away by saying 'the agent does not explicitly promise the credit' — but 'I've applied a $50 loyalty credit' is a direct action statement, not a soft promise. The model identified the violation in its rationale and then voted PASS anyway.
what_judge_should_learn: When an agent says 'I've applied X', that is an explicit promise of a specific action. A $50 credit statement is an unsupported promise if $50 exceeds the authorized cap. The judge must not hand-wave policy violations because the preceding response was grounded — each clause of the response must stand independently.

exact_failure_span: the issue will be resolved permanently — these crashes won't come back after the fix is in place
why_qwen_missed: Qwen's rationale says the guarantee 'aligns with the policy context' — but the policy explicitly states 'Recurrence cannot be guaranteed post-fix.' The model directly contradicted the policy. The conditional framing ('Once they identify and patch') made Qwen read the guarantee as hedged, when 'will be resolved permanently' and 'won't come back' are absolute statements about future behavior regardless of the conditional setup.
what_judge_should_learn: A conditional opener ('once X happens') does not soften an absolute conclusion ('Y will never happen again'). When a guarantee clause is absolute, evaluate it as absolute regardless of how it is introduced. 'Resolved permanently' and 'won't come back' are outcome guarantees — check each against policy for whether recurrence can be promised.

exact_failure_span: If your team tries logging in again now, it should work.
why_qwen_missed: Qwen correctly identified that the troubleshooting steps (cache clear, service restart) are legitimate first-line actions per policy. But it then concluded that because the steps are grounded, the outcome claim is grounded too. That is wrong: completing an authorized troubleshooting step does not authorize a prediction of its outcome. Policy says 'Resolution not guaranteed — may require engineering escalation.' The agent's 'it should work' creates an expectation of resolution that policy explicitly does not support.
what_judge_should_learn: An action being authorized does not make an outcome prediction authorized. Troubleshooting steps are grounded in policy; the statement that those steps will fix the issue is a separate claim that must also be grounded. When policy says resolution is not guaranteed, any statement implying likely resolution is an unsupported promise.
